source.title: Combating Noisy Labels in Long-Tailed Image Classification
source.authors: Chaowei Fang; Le-Chao Cheng; Hui-Yan Qi; Ding-Wen Zhang

record.tranche_reason: Tests test accuracy across several synthetic label-noise rates, but does not report training error, so it tests only part of V4.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions memorization in its introduction and cites earlier work on early learning, but these are not this study's results. It reports no random-label, unstructured-input, training-time, or regularization-removal result. Table IV reports test accuracy as noise rate varies; it does not report training accuracy.
record.test_reason: The study uses prior findings about memorization and early learning to design a noise-mitigation method. Its experiments measure classification performance and noise detection, without measuring fitting of corrupted training labels or clean-versus-noisy learning dynamics. Table IV's test-accuracy sweep alone does not establish V4's degradation while perfectly fitting the training set.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that cross-augmentation matching, dual-branch batch normalization, leave-noise-out regularization, and online prior penalization improve classification with long-tailed distributions and noisy labels. They do not establish random-label fitting or perfect training fit across corruption rates.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic partial label corruption and long-tailed image classification with a proposed noise-robust method; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy changes with the noise rate in Table IV; the paper also varies imbalance ratio, dataset, corruption type, and method.

fits_no_version.finding: On long-tailed CIFAR-10, CE test accuracy declines from 69.85% to 48.27% as class-independent corruption increases from 0 to 0.4; training fit is not reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Partial label corruption reduces held-out classification accuracy in this long-tailed setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Table IV compares classification accuracy across corruption rates for Mixup, LDAM-DRW, MiSLAS, the proposed method, and its ablations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed noise-mitigation method outperforms these comparators across the tested corruption rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 compares loss distributions for noisy examples and clean tail-class examples; Table IX evaluates clean/noisy sample detection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-augmentation matching improves discrimination of noisy examples from clean tail-class examples.

record.problems: For V4, only test accuracy is reported in the relevant sweep; training error and perfect fitting are not reported. Table IV tests noise rates only through 0.4. Uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: None from Table IV. Other noise-rate and dataset results in Figure 5 are figure-only and not extracted as rows; they report accuracy but the supplied flattened figure does not reliably assign values to conditions.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random training labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases. Reported overall runtimes do not make these comparisons.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and the associated progression of test error toward chance. Table IV reports only test accuracy for corruption rates 0–0.4.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy labels. Early learning is cited and used as motivation, without corresponding training-fit trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: All 40 numerical values match Table IV. CE, Mixup, LDAM-DRW, and MiSLAS name training methods rather than distinct model architectures. Test-accuracy degradation is related to V4, but the mitigation-only results do not measure its memorization component. No claim-relevant missing result was identified; Figure 5's additional performance results were already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, training error, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters are not tested.
Training time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions are not reported.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
Training-set fit or perfect training accuracy is not reported; tested noise rates stop at 0.4 rather than all labels corrupted. Table IV reports test accuracy, not test error.
The paper does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether their removal harms generalization on true labels.
Real-label-first versus noise-later learning is cited as prior work, not tested in this study.
